title: El, la, un, una: el género
summary: Grammatical gender, the articles el/la and un/una, and the classic exceptions

blocks.title: Every noun has a gender
blocks.body: In Spanish every noun is **masculine** or **feminine**, and its article must match. The reliable clue: nouns ending in **-o** are usually masculine (**el/un**), nouns ending in **-a** are usually feminine (**la/una**). *el libro* (the book), *la mesa* (the table).

pairs.note: *el café* = the coffee (that one). *un café* = a coffee (order me one). Both must match the noun's gender.

blocks.title: The traps you have to just learn
blocks.body: The -o/-a clue is *usually* right, but Spanish loves exceptions. Some **-a words are masculine**: *el problema, el día, el mapa, el idioma*. Some **-o words are feminine**: *la mano, la foto, la moto*. And nouns ending in -e or a consonant go either way (*la calle*, *el coche*). When unsure, learn the noun **with its article**.
blocks.callout: Learn *la mano* and *el día* as whole units now — they trip up everyone forever otherwise.

blocks.explain: *el problema* — masculine despite the -a. Words like *problema, tema, idioma* (often from Greek) are masculine. A classic trap.
*la mano* — feminine despite the -o. Pair it with *la foto* and *la moto* in the same 'exceptions' box.
